2. Exclusion

2.1.1 Decision makers must consider whether there are serious reasons to apply one (or more) of the exclusion clauses. Each case must be considered on its individual facts.

2.1.2 If the person is excluded from the Refugee Convention, they will also be excluded from a grant of humanitarian protection, which has a wider range of exclusions than refugee status.

2.1.3 For guidance on exclusion and restricted leave, see the Asylum Instruction on Exclusion under Articles 1F and 33(2) of the Refugee Convention, Humanitarian Protection and the instruction on Restricted Leave.

3. Convention reason(s)

3.1.1 Actual or imputed political opinion.

3.1.2 Establishing a convention reason is not sufficient to be recognised as a refugee. The question is whether the person has a well-founded fear of persecution on account of an actual or imputed Refugee Convention reason.

3.1.3 For further guidance on the 5 Refugee Convention grounds, see the Asylum Instruction, Assessing Credibility and Refugee Status.

4. Risk

4.1.1 Supporters, members and individuals engaged in low-level political activities on behalf or in support of political parties in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq (KRI) are, in general, unlikely to face a real risk of persecution or serious harm from the state. The onus is on the person to demonstrate otherwise.

4.1.2 However, political opposition figures, journalists, high-profile activists and outspoken critics of the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG), are likely to face adverse attention from the authorities or party-affiliated security actors. However, available evidence indicates that this can take a variety of different forms and does not demonstrate that treatment is sufficiently serious, widespread or systematic to establish a generalised real risk. Accordingly, the onus remains on a person who falls within one of these profiles to show that they would be at risk of persecution or serious harm based on their specific circumstances.

4.1.3 The Kurdistan Region of Iraq (KRI) is a semi-autonomous region with its own president, prime minister, cabinet and parliament, although it remains subject to the Constitution of Federal Iraq. Political power has long been dominated by the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK), which remain the principal political actors in the region. Political leadership within both parties remains largely concentrated within two prominent families: the Barzani family, which leads the KDP and is based in Erbil, and the Talabani family, which leads the PUK and is based in Sulaymaniyah (see Legal context, Political system and The Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) – the ruling parties).

4.1.4 The KDP and PUK have governed the region through a power-sharing arrangement since 2006, despite periods of tension and a history of armed conflict. Sources describe KRI politics as characterised by rivalry and competition between the two parties, which maintain distinct areas of influence and extensive patronage networks across political, economic, security, media and public institutions. The most recent parliamentary elections took place in October 2024, with the KDP remaining the largest party with 39 seats and the PUK the second largest with 23, although neither party secured a parliamentary majority. Sources indicate that relations between the KDP and PUK deteriorated following the elections, contributing to a prolonged deadlock over power-sharing arrangements and delaying the formation of a new regional government. While reporting from August 2026 suggested that negotiations had resumed and some progress had been made, no new Kurdish Regional Government (KRG) had been formed at the time of writing (see Political system and The Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) – the ruling parties, October 2024 Parliamentary Elections).

4.1.5 Available evidence indicates that political opposition continues to operate within the KRI and that some level of criticism of the authorities is tolerated. Opposition parties participate in elections, hold parliamentary seats and publicly criticise the ruling parties. However, sources indicate that opposition politicians and activists have at times occasionally faced harassment, detention and, in some reported cases, physical abuse by security forces. Sources have also reported restrictions on the activities of some opposition parties and media outlets, while other sources documented arrests, short-term detentions and alleged mistreatment of activists linked to opposition parties. Several incidents were reportedly linked to criticism of the authorities, allegations of corruption, or participation in protests (see Opposition politicians).

4.1.6 During 2025, several prominent opposition figures were arrested or prosecuted, including Lahur Sheikh Jangi Talabany of the People’s Front, Shaswar Abdulwahid of the New Generation Movement and Aram Qadr of the National Coalition. Authorities maintained that these arrests and prosecutions were undertaken on criminal or security-related grounds, while supporters alleged that they were politically motivated and formed part of a broader pattern of repression. Arrests of political opposition figures continued into 2026. Sources also reported pressure on opposition campaigning, alongside concerns about due process and judiciary independence (see The New Generation Movement (NGM), Other parties and Opposition politicians).

11. Media environment

11.1 Political affiliation of media outlets

11.1.1 In January 2024, MEI published an article entitled ‘Partisan press: The dominance of party-backed media in Iraq’s Kurdistan Region’ which stated:

‘… [M]edia coverage in the Kurdistan Region largely promotes the interests of politically motivated patrons, rather than performing a public service mission of providing impartial and high-quality information to all audiences.

‘There are some independent outlets, but they have limited reach due to lack of funding and harassment by the authorities. Their work ends up drowned out by the party-funded enterprises. For both the Kurdish public and foreign observers, this skews the playing field and creates a biased perception of events and what issues are important.

‘Moreover, the resulting system produces reporting that is centered on the daily activities of the political elite, rather than stories that tackle systemic problems like corruption, the economy, environmental degradation, and human rights abuses. When these issues are covered by partisan outlets, they are framed to highlight the most positive possible interpretation or used to score points against political opponents.’[footnote 40]

11.1.2 BBC Monitoring’s media guide for Iraq, updated in March 2026, stated:

‘The media in the northern Kurdistan Region reflect the political divisions in the semi-autonomous area, where most of the main outlets are affiliated with the rival political parties of the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) and its opposition.

‘… TV is the main medium in the Kurdistan Region, and social media are popular for Kurdish-related news, Facebook in particular. Kurdish media have separate social media accounts for their various language sections.

‘Irbil [Erbil] is home to the main pro-Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) outlets, while Sulaymaniyah is the base for pro-Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) and other non-KDP media.

‘Pro-KDP outlets belonging to the Rudaw Media Network and those of the Kurdistan24 (K24) for Media and Research dominate the Kurdish broadcast and digital media. They are considered to be separately affiliated with Kurdistan Region President Nechirvan Barzani and his cousin, KRG Prime Minister Masrour Barzani.

‘… In Kurdistan Region, prominent outlets say they are “independent” and owned by private companies. However, their political affiliations and support for specific politicians are known to audiences, and their political bias is clear from their coverage.

‘Political affiliation in the Kurdish media is more obvious during times of heightened political tension, notably before and during nationwide and regional parliamentary elections. The partiality can be blatant in the post-election phase as Kurdish groupings attempt to form government cabinets.

‘… Non-partisan and opposition journalists in Iraqi Kurdistan … accuse the ruling KDP and PUK of controlling the Kurdistan Journalists Syndicate, the journalists’ union in the region, by fielding their members as union officials and agreeing beforehand on dividing up posts.

‘… Key pro-KDP Kurdish outlets include Rudaw TV and its multilingual digital platforms. Rudaw’s main competitor is another pro-KDP private channel, Kurdistan24 (K24) TV and its digital platforms. They serve regional and international audiences in Arabic, English and Turkish, in addition to the main Kurdish languages. K24 has pages in Farsi and other languages. Ava News is the third largest pro-KDP outlet in the region based on social media followers.

‘Other key Kurdish outlets include opposition pro-New Generation Movement (NGM) NRT TV, pro-PUK Khandan (Xendan) website, and the PUK’s Kurdsat News TV. Channel8 TV is an emerging pro-PUK channel, but has a smaller social media following than established outlets.

‘… Nechirvan Barzani was elected as president of the semi-autonomous Kurdistan Region in 2019, having been prime minister for several years. He is the KDP’s first deputy leader.

‘Nechirvan is the ultimate owner of the Rudaw Media Network, which runs TV and radio stations, a multilingual website, and social media. When Rudaw TV was launched in 2013, it carried extensive coverage of news about him.

‘… Before becoming the KRG prime minister in 2019, Masrour Barzani was the chancellor of the Kurdistan Region Security Council (KRSC), and before that, the chief of the Parastin intelligence agency of the KDP.

‘… Masrour Barzani is seen as the ultimate owner of K24 TV, although the station does not link its ownership to him. K24 is Rudaw’s main competitor. Its co-founder and director until 2019, Noreldin Waisy, is the prime minister’s media secretary.

‘K24 promotes Masrour Barzani and covers his domestic activities, foreign trips and news conferences. His social media posts are promoted via the TV and its website.

‘… Shaswar Abdulwahid, a construction and media businessman turned politician and head of the opposition party New Generation Movement (NGM), is considered the ultimate owner of Nalia Radio and TV (NRT) and affiliated outlets.

‘NRT news channel broadcasts his news conferences and Q&As. It airs anti-government criticisms and reports on rivalries between the ruling Kurdish parties.

‘… Ahead of the October 2024 parliamentary election in the Kurdistan Region, the Kurdish media’s TikTok outlets were flooded with election propaganda from the parties they are affiliated with.

‘… Rudaw was considered to be pro-Turkey in its early years, in line with KDP party’s policies. It continues to relay Turkish official news and live news conferences of the Turkish president and his party’s rallies, especially when they touch on Kurdish affairs.
